prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday. Bless the word week, its seven small days trail with y. Bless the men whose words I was too young to hear. A whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief, I have so little left to borrow. But my hair, it grows— if hair be gold, cut mine so I might rid my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves, universities, those hands caress what’s not theirs. Bless thinking it was yours. Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train before and after me as they blush, as they transfer into tunnels for the red line. Oh bless, bless wildly, what remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, the ones who didn’t. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, fragile fortress, my friend’s body absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying If you’re going through hell, Hello.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Bless, Tuesday, Monday

outputs.L1: Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday. Bless the word *week*, its seven small days trailing with *y*. Bless the men whose words I was too young to hear. A whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief; I have so little left to borrow. But my hair—it grows. If hair be gold, cut mine so that I might rid my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves, universities—those hands that caress what is not theirs. Bless believing it was yours. Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them for holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train, before and after me, as they blush, as they transfer through tunnels to the red line. Oh, bless—bless wildly—what remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, and the ones who did not. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, fragile fortress; bless my friend’s body, absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying, “If you’re going through hell, hello.”
outputs.L2: Praise Monday and Tuesday alike. Honor the word *week*, followed by seven brief names that all end in *y*. Give thanks for the men who spoke when I was still too young to understand them. Canals welcome murmurs. Cherish my laughter, borrowed from sorrow when almost nothing else remains available to me. Still, my hair keeps lengthening; if it truly counts as treasure, shear it off and use its worth to free the person I love from student debt. Praise the takers, and the universities whose hands fondle possessions that never belonged to them. Praise the belief that something was ever yours. Beloved, these hands are here; bless them as they keep the door open. Honor everyone who weeps on the F train, before me and after, reddening as they pass through underground corridors to change to the red line. Bless without restraint all the work still unfinished. Bless whoever warned me, and whoever stayed silent. Even shallow breathing offers benediction. Honor frailty—that delicate stronghold—and my friend’s unhealthy body. Bless the voice of a dependable person who picks up when you call and greets you amid your suffering: “If you’re passing through hell—hello.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker discovers reasons to bless the ordinary: passing time, everyday language, and small moments that might otherwise go unnoticed. This attention to the commonplace suggests that meaning and beauty do not depend on extraordinary experiences; they can be found in the simple details of daily life. Although grief has changed the speaker—shaping even the sound and character of their laughter—it has not eliminated the possibility of growth. Generosity, tenderness, and the desire to care for others continue to endure alongside sorrow.

At the same time, the poem critiques universities and other institutions that encourage ideals of service and selflessness while exploiting the very people expected to embody those values. This contradiction exposes the gap between public moral language and actual institutional behavior. Against such systems, the poem presents shared vulnerability as a source of solidarity. Sorrow can connect strangers as well as friends, revealing common needs beneath social differences. Ultimately, the poem suggests that dependable human connection offers one of the strongest forms of comfort during suffering: the presence of others may not erase grief, but it can provide companionship, recognition, and the strength to continue.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts the pressures of ordinary life through a long, cascading litany of blessings. Grief, debt, illness, exploitation, and vulnerability appear not as isolated crises but as conditions that overlap and accumulate. By repeatedly blessing people, objects, losses, and modest acts of care, the speaker transforms the traditional language of prayer into a way of acknowledging experiences that are often ignored or treated as shameful. Nothing is too painful, mundane, or damaged to be named.

The poem’s repeated blessings do not deny suffering or offer easy consolation. Instead, they insist on looking directly at weakness, dependence, and uncertainty. Financial hardship, bodily fragility, emotional loss, and the fear of being used by others remain real. Yet the act of naming these experiences gives them dignity. The poem suggests that grace does not always arrive as rescue or resolution; sometimes it appears simply as recognition—the assurance that one’s pain has been seen and that one is not alone in carrying it.

Humor also plays an important role in this vision. The movement between serious hardship and ordinary, sometimes comic details keeps the poem from becoming hopeless or sentimental. Laughter becomes a form of endurance, a way of preserving freedom in circumstances that might otherwise feel overwhelming. By placing jokes, friendships, practical objects, and small gestures beside illness and grief, the poem shows how resilience is often built from seemingly minor things.

Above all, the poem locates hope in human connection. Friendship and dependable care provide a counterweight to exploitation, loneliness, and fear. The repeated act of blessing becomes an expression of solidarity, gathering the vulnerable into a shared community rather than leaving them isolated. Even weakness can become a source of grace when it allows people to recognize their need for one another.

The poem therefore offers no promise that suffering will disappear. Its hope is quieter and more durable: that grief can be spoken, vulnerability can be honored, and hardship can be met with humor and companionship. What finally matters is the presence of someone who reliably answers when called. In that response—in the simple fact of one person reaching another—the poem discovers a form of resilience strong enough to endure loss.
outputs.L5: Monday opens the door to a fresh week, while Tuesday brings another chance to move forward. May God bless both Monday and Tuesday with peace, strength, and new opportunities. Let every day be a reminder that small steps can lead to great progress.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem built around the repeated word “Bless,” exploring grief, friendship, student debt, illness, and small acts of kindness on the New York subway.
counterfactuals.output:
Bless the friend who answers at 2 a.m., voice frayed with sleep but steady enough to hold your grief while it shakes its wet coat in the hallway. Bless the dead, who keep misplacing themselves in songs, in grocery aisles, in the blue cup you cannot throw away. Bless the living, bewildered by the rent, by the diagnosis, by the monthly email that says your student loan is due—as if knowledge were a country you escaped and must keep paying ransom to.

Bless the body, its mutinies and mercies. Bless the pill split carefully on the kitchen counter, the insurance form, the waiting room fish tank where everything bright swims behind glass. Bless the friend who comes to the appointment with bad coffee and worse jokes, who writes down what the doctor says because fear has turned your mind into a station where no train stops.

Bless the subway, iron animal beneath the city, carrying our private winters. Bless the woman who holds the doors though the conductor scolds. Bless the teenager who gives his seat to the man with the cane and pretends he was getting off anyway. Bless the stranger who gathers spilled oranges before they roll onto the tracks. Bless the hand that points—uptown is that side—the MetroCard passed back through the emergency gate, the headphones lifted to hear someone ask for help.

Bless the stalled train between stations, where for one dark minute we see each other reflected in the windows: tired nurse, adjunct professor, coughing child, man asleep over a backpack full of cans. Bless whoever shares a tissue. Bless whoever looks away kindly. Bless whoever looks directly and does not turn suffering into spectacle.

Bless our debts, though they do not deserve it: the numbers blooming interest in locked rooms, the education we carry like a library on fire. Bless the friends who split the check by what each person ate, who say pay me whenever and mean it, who slip twenty dollars into a coat pocket and never confess.

Bless grief, not because it is holy, but because it proves the door once opened. Bless friendship, the lamp left on beside it. Bless illness, only for teaching us the fierce grammar of enough: enough breath, enough soup, enough morning.

Bless the city that bruises and bandages with the same hands. Bless the train arriving at last, its windows lit like a row of small, stubborn promises. Bless us boarding. Bless us making room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary free-verse poem that uses anaphora, surreal wordplay, and dark humor. Include hair imagined as gold, universities as thieves, the F train, a sick friend, and someone answering the phone during a crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
Because her hair was gold—  
not blonde, not honey,  
but bullion braided against bankruptcy—  
we trusted her with the light.

Because the universities were thieves  
with ivy-colored gloves,  
they stole our twenties politely,  
mailed us receipts called diplomas,  
then asked for donations.

Because the F train stalled  
between stations,  
the conductor apologized  
in the voice of a weather app  
predicting a ninety percent chance  
of never arriving.

Because our sick friend texted  
*still sick lol*  
from a bed that had begun  
collecting him like evidence,  
we brought soup, cheap flowers,  
and the kind of jokes  
that cough when they laugh.

Because the crisis had excellent timing—  
smoke in the kitchen, sirens downstairs,  
the moon filing for custody of the night—  
Mara answered her phone.

“Hello?”

As if hello were a bucket.  
As if hello had a fire extinguisher.  
As if hello, under the circumstances,  
had not already left the building.

Because someone always answers  
when the world is ending,  
because someone always says  
*Can I call you back?*  
while the ceiling rehearses its collapse,  
we laughed.

We laughed until the F train moved.  
We laughed until the universities  
picked our pockets again.  
We laughed until our friend  
closed his eyes—not forever,  
he clarified, Jesus—  
just for a minute.

And because her hair was gold,  
the dark came closer  
with a pair of scissors.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a blessing-poem for ordinary and painful things—weekdays, weak breaths, borrowed laughter, fragile bodies, strangers holding doors, and voices crying underground. End with a pun involving “hell” and “hello.”
counterfactuals.output:
Bless Monday, still buttoning its gray coat,  
and Tuesday, carrying yesterday’s ache.  
Bless every weekday that arrives unpraised  
and works its small shift in the heart.  

Bless the weak breath—  
its thin candle, its stubborn flame.  
Bless laughter borrowed from a friend,  
worn awhile like a warm, bright scarf.  

Bless these fragile bodies:  
hinge and bruise, hunger and bone,  
each one a breakable cup  
still daring to hold sweetness.  

Bless strangers who keep doors from closing,  
who wait one second longer than required,  
making of an ordinary hand  
a brief and golden shelter.  

Bless the voices crying underground,  
beneath rubble, silence, fear—  
may every listening ear become a shovel,  
every answer a rope toward morning.  

Bless all who stand at sorrow’s gate  
and, hearing only hell,  
add one small, saving syllable—  
and answer: **hello.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem in a tender, incantatory voice. Repeat “Bless” throughout, mix grief with absurdity, and move associatively from language and memory to student loans, subway tunnels, friendship, and survival.
counterfactuals.output:
Bless the word before it learns what it means.  
Bless its little coat of vowels, its pockets full of weather.  
Bless the tongue, that pink archivist, misfiling every kiss.

I remember you saying remember, and the room tilted softly,  
a bowl carrying its one cracked pear.

Bless the crack.  
Bless the pear for continuing its yellow work.  
Bless memory, that unreliable subway map,  
all its stations renamed after the dead,  
all its arrows pointing: *You were here, you were here, you were—*

Then the letter arrived about my student loans,  
formal as a swan in a necktie.  
It said Dear Borrower, as if borrowing were a country  
and I its minor, bewildered prince.

Bless the interest accruing in the night  
like intelligent mold.  
Bless the zeroes breeding quietly behind the decimal.  
Bless my degree in holding a paper cup  
while the future leaks through.

Underground, the train screams in its sleep.  
Bless the tunnels, their black intestines,  
their rats dragging pizza toward a private heaven.  
Bless the woman applying lipstick in the window’s dark.  
Bless the man singing off-key to no one,  
which is another name for everyone.

At Canal Street I mistake a stranger for you  
and grief puts on its ridiculous hat—  
feathers, bells, one plastic cherry.

Bless grief’s hat.  
Bless its terrible fashion.  
Bless how it enters without knocking  
then asks if there’s any mustard.

Friend, you once split your last orange with me  
on a staircase smelling of rain and old mail.  
Bless the half you pressed into my hand.  
Bless the seeds we spat into a coffee tin,  
certain we had invented spring.

We have survived by such ceremonies:  
a text at 2:13 saying home?  
a borrowed sock, a soup with too much salt,  
the lie *I’m fine* carried gently between us  
like an injured bird that may yet become a bird.

Bless the may yet.  
Bless the almost.  
Bless the body, its stubborn committee of sparks.  
Bless the lungs ringing their wet blue bells.  
Bless the heart, absurd fist,  
knocking and knocking on the locked door of morning.

And if morning does not answer,  
bless the knocking.

Bless the hand beside the hand.  
Bless the tunnel for having two ends,  
even when we can see neither.

Bless the word survival—  
its torn hem, its grocery-store flowers,  
its mouth full of borrowed light.

Bless us, then, not for being unbroken,  
but for breaking into one another’s darkness  
and calling that sound a language.

Bless. Bless.  
The train is coming.

Bless the train.

Bless the coming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a compact poem about finding sacredness in loss and precarity? Use dense internal rhyme, unexpected metaphors, references to Monday and Tuesday, the F train and red line, and conclude with the comfort of a reliable person picking up the phone.
counterfactuals.output:
Monday, loss glosses the F train’s steel—  
a thin hymn, brake-shriek turned reliquary.  
Tuesday, the red line threads its bright wound  
through town: ruin as rosary, rent as rite.

We balance—chalice on a fire escape—  
each ache a small, unsteady altar.  
Still, when the night unbuttons its last light,  
you pick up the phone. You always do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
